subject: Automotive & EVs
title: The Four-Stroke Cycle
description: A quick win: understand The Four-Stroke Cycle.

hook.text: Every gasoline engine repeats four steps—intake, compression, power, exhaust—thousands of times a minute.

buildup.text: First the piston drops, sucking in fuel and air. Then it rises to squeeze the mixture tight.

discovery.text: A spark ignites the compressed mix, slamming the piston down—that single stroke moves the car.

twist.text: Only one of the four strokes produces power. The other three just prepare and clean up.

climax.text: Nikolaus Otto patented this cycle in 1876, and nearly every gasoline engine still uses it today.

punchline.text: One stroke does the work, three strokes set it up.

quiz.question: How many of the four strokes actually produce power?

details.summary: The four-stroke cycle of intake, compression, power, and exhaust converts fuel combustion into rotational motion through four distinct piston movements, forming the operating principle of virtually every car engine since 1876.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding the four-stroke cycle is the foundation of all engine science. Every improvement in engine technology from turbocharging to variable valve timing modifies this basic cycle.
takeaways: Intake draws air and fuel into the cylinder
Compression squeezes the mixture for efficient combustion
Power and exhaust strokes extract work and clear spent gases

faq.question: Who invented the four-stroke engine?
faq.answer: Nikolaus Otto patented the first practical four-stroke engine in 1876, though Alphonse Beau de Rochas described the theoretical cycle in 1862. Otto successfully commercialized the design that bears his name.

faq.question: Why four strokes instead of two?
faq.answer: Four strokes provide dedicated phases for each function, resulting in more complete combustion, lower emissions, and better fuel economy. Two-stroke engines fire every revolution but waste more fuel through less controlled scavenging.
